[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Security Groups and Network ACLs in AWS"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Amazon Web Services (AWS) provides two key features for controlling network traffic in your Virtual Private Cloud (VPC): Security Groups and Network Access Control Lists (Network ACLs). Understanding the differences and how to use them effectively is crucial for securing your AWS infrastructure."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Security Groups"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Security Groups act as a virtual firewall for your EC2 instances. They control inbound and outbound traffic at the instance level. Think of them as a gatekeeper for each individual instance."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Stateful: Security Groups are stateful, meaning that if you allow inbound traffic on a specific port, the outbound traffic in response to that inbound traffic is automatically allowed, regardless of outbound rules. The reverse is also true. If you allow outbound traffic, the inbound response is automatically allowed."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Allow Rules Only: Security Groups only support 'allow' rules. You cannot explicitly deny traffic."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Applied at the Instance Level: Security Groups are associated with individual EC2 instances."},{"order":8,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Evaluated Before Instance Launch: Security Group rules are evaluated before the traffic reaches the instance."},{"order":9,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Default Security Group: Every VPC has a default security group. If you don't specify a security group when launching an instance, it's automatically associated with the default security group. By default, the default security group allows all outbound traffic and denies all inbound traffic."},{"order":10,"type":"code","text":"# Example Security Group Rule (Allowing SSH access)
Type: SSH
Protocol: TCP
Port Range: 22
Source: 0.0.0.0/0 (All IP addresses - NOT recommended for production)"},{"order":11,"type":"subheading","text":"Network ACLs (Network Access Control Lists)"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"Network ACLs are an optional layer of security that acts as a firewall for controlling traffic in and out of one or more subnets. They operate at the subnet level, providing a broader level of control than Security Groups."},{"order":13,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Stateless: Network ACLs are stateless, meaning that inbound and outbound rules must be explicitly defined. If you allow inbound traffic on a specific port, you must also create a corresponding outbound rule to allow the response traffic. If you don't, the response will be blocked."},{"order":14,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Allow and Deny Rules: Network ACLs support both 'allow' and 'deny' rules, giving you more granular control over traffic."},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Applied at the Subnet Level: Network ACLs are associated with subnets."},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Evaluated Before Traffic Enters/Exits Subnet: Network ACL rules are evaluated before traffic enters or exits the subnet."},{"order":17,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Default Network ACL: Every VPC has a default network ACL that allows all inbound and outbound traffic. You can modify the default network ACL, but it's generally recommended to create custom network ACLs."},{"order":18,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Rule Numbers: Network ACL rules are evaluated in order, starting with the lowest numbered rule. Once a rule matches, it's applied, and no further rules are evaluated. It's best practice to leave gaps in the rule numbers (e.g., 100, 110, 120) to allow for future rule additions."},{"order":19,"type":"code","text":"# Example Network ACL Rule (Allowing HTTP access)
Rule Number: 100
Type: Inbound
Protocol: TCP
Port Range: 80
Source: 0.0.0.0/0
Action: Allow

# Example Network ACL Rule (Denying access from a specific IP)
Rule Number: 110
Type: Inbound
Protocol: TCP
Port Range: All
Source: 203.0.113.0/24
Action: Deny"},{"order":20,"type":"subheading","text":"Key Differences Summarized"},{"order":21,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Security Groups: Stateful, Allow rules only, Instance level."},{"order":22,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Network ACLs: Stateless, Allow and Deny rules, Subnet level."},{"order":23,"type":"subheading","text":"Best Practices"},{"order":24,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use Security Groups as your primary firewall mechanism for EC2 instances."},{"order":25,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use Network ACLs for an additional layer of security at the subnet level, especially if you need to explicitly deny traffic."},{"order":26,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Follow the principle of least privilege: Only allow the minimum necessary traffic to and from your resources."},{"order":27,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Regularly review and update your Security Group and Network ACL rules to ensure they are still appropriate for your application's needs."},{"order":28,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Avoid using 0.0.0.0/0 (allowing all IP addresses) as the source for inbound rules in production environments. Instead, restrict access to specific IP addresses or CIDR blocks."},{"order":29,"type":"paragraph","text":"By understanding and effectively utilizing Security Groups and Network ACLs, you can significantly enhance the security posture of your AWS environment."}]
